title: Australia raises rates despite weakening housing as the inflation return slips into 2027
summary: Australia’s Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85% on November 3. Six members supported the increase and three preferred to leave the rate at 4.60%. The majority acted despite falling house prices and a rising unemployment rate because the inflation outlook had deteriorated. The Board judged that inflation would stay above 3% for the coming year and reach the top of its 2–3% range only in late 2027, around three quarters later than previously expected. It identified a risk that a prolonged period of high inflation would start to shape the prices and wages people expect in future.

The statement gave several reasons why the Board did not look through the entire increase as a temporary fuel shock. The Middle East conflict and disruptions to oil supply had pushed up fuel and other commodity costs. Higher fuel costs were beginning to pass into other prices. Domestic capacity pressure was also a little greater than the Board had previously estimated, and AI-related investment was increasing the price of technology goods. Its liaison contacts reported firms already raising selling prices or planning to pass on costs. A planned increase and a price that customers actually pay provide different evidence about persistence. The Board said that some measures of expectations had risen, without identifying a uniform shift across all measures or horizons.

Earlier rate increases had already tightened financial conditions. The Board expected a further slowdown in output, which would reduce pressure on capacity. Higher borrowing costs and weaker housing prices and turnover were expected to restrain household consumption and dwelling investment. The housing channel therefore concerned both current spending and future construction. By contrast, the Board expected stronger near-term business investment, including spending related to data centres. One interest-rate-sensitive part of the economy could weaken while another continued to draw on scarce resources.

The labour outlook contained another apparent tension. The unemployment rate had already increased and the Board expected it to rise more than it had anticipated in August. Yet it still expected employment to grow. The two statements can coexist if the labour force grows faster than employment. The release itself did not quantify the contribution of labour-force growth or claim that job creation had stopped. Assessing the employment side of the mandate consequently requires evidence beyond the change in the unemployment rate.

The largest external risks did not all point in the same direction for policy. Prolonged energy disruption could keep inflation high while lowering Australian and overseas growth. Trading-partner growth had so far been stronger than anticipated, as AI-related investment outweighed adverse effects of the conflict. The statement also pointed to weak Australian productivity as a constraint on potential output and uncertainty about how far the housing downturn would spread. A further deterioration in consumption would imply a different balance of risks from persistent cost pass-through and resilient demand.

The vote records disagreement over the decision taken that day. The release gives the counts for each setting, and it gives the Board’s collective account of the case for tightening. It does not state why each member voted as they did. For the next decision the Board retained discretion to respond to incoming evidence about inflation, employment and the outlook. The release provides neither a subsequent rate path nor the market probability assigned to November’s increase beforehand.

questions.question: Are higher costs showing up in final prices across the economy?
questions.detail: Compare fuel and commodity price changes with realised prices for services and non-energy goods. Follow the firms reporting intentions in liaison through their next price review. If planned increases fail to stick as demand weakens, the persistence risk would be smaller than the initial reports suggest.

questions.question: Where are higher rates constraining demand most sharply?
questions.detail: Separate changes in borrowing costs from declines in housing prices and turnover. Compare household consumption and dwelling investment with business investment in data centres. Check whether weakness spreads beyond housing-sensitive sectors or is offset by investment that competes for the same workers and inputs.

questions.question: Does higher unemployment reflect weaker hiring or more people seeking work?
questions.detail: Track the labour force, employment, vacancies and hours together. Positive job growth with faster labour-force expansion yields a different income and wage outlook from outright job losses. Compare actual outcomes against expectations held at the time rather than interpreting later revisions as evidence that was already available.

questions.question: What would distinguish news about the next move from news about the November vote?
questions.detail: Compare dated short-rate expectations immediately before and after the release across several meeting dates. Record the timing of simultaneously published projections and the subsequent press conference before assigning a yield change to the six-to-three vote. The decision statement itself supplies neither those prices nor the members’ individual policy paths.

limitation: This manuscript covers the Board’s November 3 decision statement. The statement records the vote and the revised return horizon but does not publish individual voters’ reasons or a market-implied path.
